claims.text: The proposed predictive approach targets refractory high-entropy alloys prepared as homogeneous, single-phase solid solutions.
A machine-learning model trained using binary-alloy descriptors can accurately predict refractory high-entropy-alloy compositions with phonon thermal conductivity below 0.1 W/(m·K).
Machine-learning models trained on binary-alloy data can be transferred to prediction tasks for multielement and high-entropy alloys.
Atomic-size difference and electronegativity difference can be used as descriptors in machine-learning models for high-entropy alloys.
Binary phase-diagram and chemical descriptors contain sufficient information to predict low phonon thermal conductivity in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Atomic-scale chemical disorder and lattice distortions act as effective phonon-scattering centers.
Atomic-size and electronegativity mismatches produce lattice distortions that enhance phonon scattering.
High-dimensional descriptors allow the model to capture chemical and structural effects overlooked by conventional averaging methods.
Conventional heuristic and rule-of-mixtures approaches rely solely on composition averages and do not account for detailed atomic-scale effects.
The proposed model will improve prediction accuracy by at least 20% relative to conventional rule-of-mixtures approaches.
The model will reliably identify alloys with measured thermal conductivity below 0.1 W/(m·K).
The approach is applicable only to single-phase solid solutions and may fail for multiphase alloys or systems with substantial defect or structural complexity.
Measurements from cryogenic to moderate temperatures will ensure or establish phase stability.
Predictions of high-entropy-alloy transport properties must be confronted with experimental measurements to assess their validity.
The exact improvement margin and generalizability across refractory high-entropy-alloy compositions remain uncertain pending experimental validation.
Laser-flash analysis or calorimetric techniques can provide the phonon thermal-conductivity measurement required by the benchmark.
The hypothesis is falsified if more than half of the synthesized alloys exceed 0.1 W/(m·K), or if accuracy improves by less than 20% over conventional methods.
